title: The Buffalo's Last Shape
hookLine: Mahisha keeps changing shape until the goddess pins him: why Durga stands on the buffalo
carry: durga on the buffalo: the goddess restores dharma
tomorrow: the gods ask why she didn't just burn him with a look. what's their answer?

cards: The generals are dead, their armies scattered. Now the buffalo himself comes onto the field.
In the third chapter Mahisha arrives in his own form, and the text makes him frightening: he tramples her troops with his hooves, flings them with his horns, lashes them with his tail.
His hooves crack the ground; his breath tosses mountains. He charges her lion. And the goddess, the text says, grows angry.
It's the scene shown in images of her as Mahishasuramardini, she who crushes the buffalo demon: a goddess, a lion, a buffalo at her feet. Here is how the text tells it.

teach.h: A BUFFALO, A LION, A MAN, AN ELEPHANT.
teach.b: She throws her noose around him, and he stops being a buffalo. He's a lion. She cuts off its head, and a man with a sword stands in its place.

She shoots him down, and he's a great elephant, dragging her lion with his trunk. She cuts off the trunk, and he's a buffalo again, shaking the worlds. Every time she has him, he becomes something else.

Then, in the middle of battle, the goddess stops and drinks from her cup, again and again, laughing, her eyes going red. Mahisha, full of his own strength, bellows and hurls mountains at her with his horns.

teach.h: ROAR FOR A MOMENT, YOU FOOL.
teach.b: In paraphrase: roar, roar for a moment, you fool, while I drink. When I've killed you, the gods will be roaring here instead.

teach.h: HALF OUT OF HIS OWN SKIN.
teach.b: Then she leaps, sets her foot on his neck and pierces him with her spear.
Pinned, he starts to come out of the buffalo's mouth in his real form, only halfway out, still fighting, and she cuts off his head with her great sword. The gods rejoice.

teach.h: DURGA ON THE BUFFALO: DHARMA RESTORED.
teach.b: This is the scene Hindus bow to at every Durga Puja: Durga, calm, her lion beside her, her foot on the buffalo. Mahisha had thrown the gods out of heaven. The goddess puts the world back in order, what Hindus call dharma.
Many teachers read the buffalo as our own ego, always changing shape, and the goddess as the power that pins it.

how: The goddess slaying Mahisha, Mahishasuramardini, is a familiar image of Durga, and during Durga Puja and Navaratri Hindus worship images that show her with her foot on the buffalo and Mahisha emerging from it; many communities celebrate her victory on Vijayadashami, the tenth day.

games.q: Nani, reading the Devi Mahatmya at Navaratri, says the buffalo demon "lives in all of us too." what does she mean?
o: many teachers read Mahisha as the ego, changing shape until the goddess pins it.
she means people are secretly buffalo.
she means demons hide in the house during the festival.
games.why: it's a reading, not the only one: Mahisha keeps changing form, the way the ego and dullness do, and the goddess's power pins him until he has to show himself.

practice: If you pray, picture Durga the way families see her at Navaratri: calm, the lion beside her, her foot on the buffalo. Bow to her, or say her name softly a few times, as many devotees do, and ask for steadiness.
If you don't pray, picture the image anyway and let the breath slow, long in like a drink, long out, unhurried, the way she was in the middle of the fight.

wordCard.voice: The Devi Mahatmya. Today, Mahisha the shape-shifter, pinned under the goddess's foot: the image families bow to at Durga Puja.

orig.note: Sanskrit: mahiṣāsura-mardinī, she who crushes the buffalo demon. A name for the goddess.

carryVoice: Your line: Durga on the buffalo, the goddess restores dharma. In the middle of the fight she stopped to drink, and wasn't hurried. Until tomorrow.
